note: 50 questions, all one level. Built for surprise while staying guessable. Every citation points at a source retrieved during research.

questions.prompt: How many people report having been discriminated against?
questions.whyCorrect: About one in five people worldwide say they have personally faced discrimination — and the rate is rising, from 14.8% to 17.1%.
whyWrong: Far too low — discrimination is reported by a fifth of people.
Vastly too low.
questions.action: Ask what counts as discrimination under the law where you live.

questions.prompt: Discrimination rates worldwide have recently:
questions.whyCorrect: Up from 14.8% to 17.1%. This is one of the SDG indicators moving in the wrong direction.
whyWrong: The trend is upward, not downward.
There was a measurable increase.
questions.action: Ask why discrimination might be rising, not falling.

questions.prompt: People with disabilities report discrimination at 28%. People without report:
questions.whyCorrect: 17% — so having a disability makes you roughly 1.6 times more likely to face discrimination.
whyWrong: That's the figure for people with disabilities.
Non-disabled people report substantially less.
questions.action: Look for one thing near you that a wheelchair user couldn't use.

questions.prompt: In the least developed countries, the discrimination rate is:
questions.whyCorrect: 24.3% — nearly one in four people, well above the 17.1% world average. Poverty and discrimination reinforce each other.
whyWrong: Far too low.
LDC rates are well above average.
questions.action: Ask how discrimination could keep someone poor.

questions.prompt: The poorest fifth of people report discrimination at 17.3%. The richest fifth report:
questions.whyCorrect: 10.3% — being poor makes you notably more likely to be treated unfairly, on top of having less.
whyWrong: That's the figure for the poorest.
The wealthiest report the lowest rates.
questions.action: Ask whether people are treated differently by how they dress.

questions.prompt: People with no formal education report discrimination at 21.4%. People with higher education report:
questions.whyCorrect: 12.7% — education is protective, which is part of why leaving school early has effects that last a lifetime.
whyWrong: That's the no-education figure.
More education correlates with less reported discrimination.
questions.action: Ask how education changes how strangers treat you.

questions.prompt: How many people worldwide are refugees or forcibly displaced?
questions.whyCorrect: 37.8 million as of mid-2024 — more than the population of Canada, all forced from home.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
A hundred times too low.
questions.action: Find a country whose population is about 37 million.

questions.prompt: The world's refugee rate is 460 per 100,000 people. In 2005 it was:
questions.whyCorrect: 153 per 100,000 — the rate has tripled in under twenty years. Displacement is at levels not seen in generations.
whyWrong: That's today's rate.
The rate has risen, so 2005 was lower.
questions.action: Ask what makes people leave home permanently.

questions.prompt: The refugee rate in 2015 was about 230 per 100,000. Today it is:
questions.whyCorrect: 460 — it has doubled since the SDGs were agreed. Every year of the goals so far has seen more displacement, not less.
whyWrong: The rate has risen since 2015.
It doubled rather than halved.
questions.action: Ask which conflicts started after 2015.

questions.prompt: Which four countries do the most refugees come from?
questions.whyCorrect: Afghanistan, Syria, Ukraine and Venezuela — three from war, one from economic and political collapse.
whyWrong: These are stable, high-income countries.
These are large countries but not top refugee origins.
questions.action: Find those four countries on a map.

questions.prompt: Sending $200 home to family costs, on average:
questions.whyCorrect: 6.7% — about $13 of every $200 vanishes in fees. The SDG target is 3%, so the world is more than double where it should be.
whyWrong: Too high for the average, though banks charge more.
Far too low — fees are substantial.
questions.action: Work out the fee on $500 at 6.7%.

questions.prompt: The SDG target for money transfer costs is 3%. The actual figure is:
questions.whyCorrect: 6.7%, up from 6.2% a year earlier. Costs are moving away from the target, not toward it.
whyWrong: Costs are well above target.
The target has not been met.
questions.action: Ask why fees rise when they're supposed to fall.

questions.prompt: Which is the most expensive way to send money home?
questions.whyCorrect: Banks charge 13.4% — more than three times the 3.9% mobile operators charge. The most established institutions are the priciest.
whyWrong: Mobile operators are the cheapest at 3.9%.
Money transfer operators charge 5.6%.
questions.action: Compare 13.4% at a bank with 3.9% on a phone.

questions.prompt: Which is the CHEAPEST way to send money home?
questions.whyCorrect: Mobile operators, at 3.9% — the only channel close to the 3% target, and the newest one.
whyWrong: Banks are the most expensive by far.
Post offices sit in the middle.
questions.action: Ask why a newer technology can charge less.

questions.prompt: Sending money digitally costs 5.3%. Sending it non-digitally costs:
questions.whyCorrect: 7.2% — cash-based transfers cost nearly two points more. People without smartphones or bank accounts pay the premium.
whyWrong: Neither channel has reached the 3% target.
That's the digital figure.
questions.action: Ask who cannot use a digital transfer.

questions.prompt: What share of the world's income goes to workers as wages?
questions.whyCorrect: 52.3% — just over half. The rest goes to owners of capital: land, buildings, machines, shares.
whyWrong: Far too high — nearly half goes to capital.
Too low — workers get just over half.
questions.action: Ask what 'income from capital' means.

questions.prompt: Labour's share of world income since 2015 has:
questions.whyCorrect: Fallen 0.6 points — sounds tiny, but it works out at about $255 less per worker per year, worldwide.
whyWrong: The share has been slipping.
There was a measurable decline.
questions.action: Ask what a 0.6% shift means across billions of workers.

questions.prompt: The falling labour income share costs the average worker roughly:
questions.whyCorrect: About $255 a year — a small percentage shift that becomes real money in a household budget.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
Ten times too high.
questions.action: Ask what $255 buys where you live.

questions.prompt: Of 108 countries measured, how many grew the incomes of their poorest 40% faster than average?
questions.whyCorrect: About 6 in 10 — genuinely encouraging. In most countries with data, the bottom is catching up rather than falling behind.
whyWrong: The majority did achieve pro-poor growth.
Around four in ten did not.
questions.action: Ask what would make the poorest gain faster than the rich.

questions.prompt: Among low and lower-middle-income countries, how many achieved faster growth for their poorest 40%?
questions.whyCorrect: Fewer than half — against 7 in 10 among richer countries. Where inequality is most damaging, it is hardest to reduce.
whyWrong: Poorer countries did notably worse than rich ones.
Some did succeed.
questions.action: Ask why reducing inequality is harder in a poor country.

questions.prompt: Among upper-middle and high-income countries, how many grew poorest incomes fastest?
questions.whyCorrect: 7 in 10 — richer countries have the tax systems and benefits to close gaps, and mostly did.
whyWrong: Most richer countries did succeed.
The majority achieved pro-poor growth.
questions.action: Name a policy that helps the poorest gain fastest.

questions.prompt: How much money flowed from richer to developing countries in 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: $429 billion, up from $290 billion in 2015 — a large rise, though still modest next to global military or fossil fuel spending.
whyWrong: Ten times too high.
Ten times too low.
questions.action: Compare $429 billion with your country's annual budget.

questions.prompt: Of $429 billion in resource flows, how much was official development aid?
questions.whyCorrect: $259 billion — 60% of the total, up from 55% in 2015. Aid is a growing share of what reaches developing countries.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
Aid is 60%, not all, of resource flows.
questions.action: Ask what counts as development aid.

questions.prompt: Which region received the most resource flows in 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: Asia, at $141 billion (32%) — ahead of Africa's $91 billion (21%), largely because Asia is far more populous.
whyWrong: Africa received $91 billion — substantial, but less than Asia.
Europe is not a major recipient.
questions.action: Compare Asia's and Africa's populations.

questions.prompt: How much reached the least developed countries in 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: $80 billion of the $429 billion total — under a fifth, for the countries with the greatest need.
whyWrong: Ten times too high.
Ten times too low.
questions.action: Work out $80 billion as a share of $429 billion.

questions.prompt: Women report gender-based discrimination at roughly what rate compared to men?
questions.whyCorrect: Twice as often. Gender remains one of the strongest predictors of who gets treated unfairly.
whyWrong: The gap is large, not absent.
Women report it far more, not less.
questions.action: Ask where gender rules are still written into law.

questions.prompt: Discrimination is reported nearly twice as often in:
questions.whyCorrect: Urban areas — nearly double the rural rate. Cities mix people from different backgrounds, which creates both opportunity and friction.
whyWrong: Rural rates are notably lower.
The urban-rural gap is substantial.
questions.action: Ask why cities might report more discrimination.

questions.prompt: Small island states saw labour's income share fall by:
questions.whyCorrect: 2.6 points — more than four times the 0.6-point global fall. Small island economies were hit hardest.
whyWrong: The share fell sharply there.
Far smaller than the actual decline.
questions.action: Ask why small island economies are so exposed.

questions.prompt: Reducing inequality between countries means:
options: Narrowing the gap in income and opportunity between rich and poor nations
questions.whyCorrect: Goal 10 targets gaps both within and between countries — a child's life chances shouldn't be set by where they were born.
whyWrong: Countries stay different; the goal is fairer outcomes.
Goal 10 explicitly calls for safe, orderly migration.
questions.action: Compare life expectancy in two countries you know.

questions.prompt: Discrimination against people with disabilities is 28% versus 17% for others. That means people with disabilities are:
options: About 1.6 times more likely to face it
questions.whyCorrect: About 1.6 times more likely — a persistent gap on top of the physical barriers they already navigate.
whyWrong: They are considerably more affected.
The ratio is about 1.6, not 10.
questions.action: Check whether your school building is fully accessible.

questions.prompt: In Central and Southern Asia, how many of 7 countries grew poorest incomes fastest?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 3 of 7 — below the global pattern. The region with a huge share of the world's poor is not closing gaps fastest.
whyWrong: Most countries in the region did not achieve this.
Some countries did succeed.
questions.action: Name three countries in Central or Southern Asia.

questions.prompt: Aid's share of resource flows rose from 55% in 2015 to:
questions.whyCorrect: 60% in 2023 — aid grew faster than loans and investment, meaning developing countries depend more on grants than before.
whyWrong: The share rose rather than fell.
Aid is a majority but not nearly all.
questions.action: Ask whether depending more on aid is good or risky.

questions.prompt: The refugee rate has tripled since 2005. This is mostly because of:
questions.whyCorrect: Conflicts in Afghanistan, Syria, Ukraine and Venezuela drove most of the increase. Refugees flee danger, not opportunity.
whyWrong: Tourists are not refugees.
The rise reflects real displacement, not just counting.
questions.action: Ask what makes someone a refugee rather than a migrant.

questions.prompt: Landlocked developing countries saw labour income share fall by:
questions.whyCorrect: 1.4 points — more than double the global decline. Landlocked countries pay more to trade and have less bargaining power.
whyWrong: Far smaller than the actual fall.
The share declined.
questions.action: Find a landlocked country and trace its route to a port.

questions.prompt: If remittance fees dropped from 6.7% to the 3% target, families would:
options: Keep roughly $7 more of every $200 sent
questions.whyCorrect: About $7 more per $200 — billions of dollars a year staying with the families who earned it rather than with intermediaries.
whyWrong: Lower fees mean more money arrives.
For families living close to the edge, it is significant.
questions.action: Multiply $7 by twelve months of transfers.

questions.prompt: Discrimination rose from 14.8% to 17.1%. In percentage terms, that increase is roughly:
questions.whyCorrect: About a 16% relative rise — a 2.3-point jump on a 14.8 base. Small-looking point changes can be large proportional moves.
whyWrong: That's the point difference, not the relative rise.
Far too high for this change.
questions.action: Practise turning point changes into percentage changes.

questions.prompt: Which regions most consistently grew the incomes of their poorest 40%?
questions.whyCorrect: Eastern and South-Eastern Asia and Europe/Northern America — the regions with the strongest growth and the strongest social systems.
whyWrong: Six in ten countries did achieve it.
This region showed weaker pro-poor growth.
questions.action: Ask what those two very different regions have in common.

questions.prompt: The world's refugee rate of 460 per 100,000 means roughly:
questions.whyCorrect: About 1 in every 217 people on Earth has been forced from home — a fill-a-stadium-every-hour scale of displacement.
whyWrong: A hundred times too low.
Ten times too high.
questions.action: Work out how many refugees a city of 200,000 would represent.

questions.prompt: Goal 10's target on migration calls for:
options: Safe, orderly and regular migration with well-managed policies
questions.whyCorrect: The goal is well-managed migration, not zero migration — dangerous irregular routes are what cost lives.
whyWrong: Goal 10 does not seek to end migration.
The aim is fair access, not access by wealth.
questions.action: Ask what makes a migration route dangerous.

questions.prompt: Bank remittance fees rose from 12.1% to 13.4%. This means:
options: The most expensive channel got more expensive
questions.whyCorrect: Already the priciest option, banks got worse — widening the gap with 3.9% mobile transfers.
whyWrong: Bank fees increased.
There was a clear 1.3-point rise.
questions.action: Ask why banks can keep charging more than competitors.

questions.prompt: Which statement about inequality does the data support?
options: Inequality within countries is falling in most measured countries, while displacement and discrimination rise
questions.whyCorrect: Goal 10 is genuinely mixed: 6 in 10 countries closing income gaps, alongside record refugees and rising discrimination.
whyWrong: Refugees and discrimination are both up sharply.
Income growth for the poorest is a real success.
questions.action: Find one Goal 10 number improving and one worsening.

questions.prompt: Aid to the least developed countries was $80 billion of $429 billion total — about:
questions.whyCorrect: About 19% — less than a fifth reaches the countries furthest behind, even though they need it most.
whyWrong: That confuses the dollar figure with a percentage.
Far too high a share.
questions.action: Ask where the other 81% goes.

questions.prompt: Latin America and the Caribbean saw labour income share fall by:
questions.whyCorrect: 1.3 points — twice the global fall, in a region already among the world's most unequal.
whyWrong: Far smaller than the actual decline.
The share fell, not rose.
questions.action: Ask why the same trend hurts unequal countries more.

questions.prompt: Mobile operators charge 3.9% for remittances, banks 13.4%. The gap suggests:
options: Competition and technology can cut costs dramatically
questions.whyCorrect: The same service costs less than a third via mobile — evidence that the target of 3% is achievable, not fantasy.
whyWrong: Mobile money is regulated and widely used.
Prices vary by provider, which is why the gap exists.
questions.action: Ask what stops everyone using the cheapest option.

questions.prompt: Post offices charge what to send money home?
questions.whyCorrect: 7.5% — between money transfer shops (5.6%) and banks (13.4%). Every channel except mobile is above the 3% target.
whyWrong: That's the bank rate.
That's the mobile operator rate.
questions.action: Rank the four channels by cost.

questions.prompt: 37.8 million forcibly displaced people is roughly equivalent to:
options: The population of a large city
questions.whyCorrect: Roughly Canada's entire population — displaced, and mostly hosted by countries that are themselves poor.
whyWrong: Vastly larger than a town.
It is far larger than any single city.
questions.action: Look up which countries host the most refugees.

questions.prompt: Total resource flows to developing countries rose from $290 billion in 2015 to:
questions.whyCorrect: $429 billion — a 48% increase in eight years, though needs grew too.
whyWrong: The rise was far larger than this.
Flows rose, they did not fall.
questions.action: Calculate the percentage rise from $290bn to $429bn.

questions.prompt: Why does the falling labour income share matter for inequality?
options: Wages are spread across billions of workers; capital income is concentrated among few owners
questions.whyCorrect: When income shifts from wages to capital, it shifts toward whoever already owns assets — so inequality widens even as the economy grows.
whyWrong: It shifts income between very different groups.
SIDS, LLDCs and Latin America saw the largest falls.
questions.action: Ask who owns the shares in the companies you buy from.

questions.prompt: Someone poor, uneducated, disabled and female faces discrimination risk that is:
options: Compounded — each factor adds to the others
questions.whyCorrect: Disadvantages stack. Each measured factor — poverty, no education, disability, gender — raises the rate on its own, and they combine.
whyWrong: Each factor independently raises the reported rate.
Protections exist but do not reverse the pattern.
questions.action: Look up what 'intersectionality' means.

questions.prompt: The most encouraging Goal 10 finding is:
options: 6 in 10 countries growing poorest incomes fastest
questions.whyCorrect: In most measured countries the bottom 40% are gaining faster than average — proof that inequality can be narrowed deliberately.
whyWrong: Displacement is at record highs.
Remittance costs are rising away from target.
questions.action: Find out what your country did for its poorest households last year.
